subject: science
title: US Middle School Science — Chemical Reactions
subtitle: Reading passages about evidence, atoms, mass, energy, reaction rate, data, and applications
description: Reading comprehension passages for a middle school physical science unit on chemical reactions. Questions mix fact retrieval, inference, explanation, data interpretation, and significance.

data.sourceTitle: What Counts as a Chemical Reaction?
data.targetTitle: What Counts as a Chemical Reaction?
data.sourcePassage: A chemical reaction happens when atoms in substances are rearranged to make new substances. The starting substances are called reactants, and the new substances are called products. This is different from a physical change, which changes size, shape, state, or appearance without making a new substance. For example, ice melting is a physical change because the substance is still water. Wood burning is a chemical change because ash, smoke, carbon dioxide, water vapor, heat, and light are produced. Scientists do not rely on one clue only. They compare observations and ask whether the evidence shows that new substances formed.

questions.question: What are the starting substances in a chemical reaction called?
questions.modelAnswer: reactants

questions.question: Which example from the passage is a physical change?
questions.modelAnswer: Ice melting is a physical change because the substance is still water.

questions.question: Why is wood burning described as a chemical change?
questions.modelAnswer: Wood burning forms new substances such as ash, smoke, carbon dioxide, and water vapor, and releases heat and light.

questions.question: Why should scientists avoid deciding from one clue only?
questions.modelAnswer: One clue can sometimes happen in a physical change, so scientists need several pieces of evidence to support the claim that new substances formed.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the difference between chemical and physical change?
questions.modelAnswer: Chemical changes form new substances, while physical changes do not.
options: Chemical changes form new substances; physical changes do not

data.sourcePassage: Common evidence of a chemical reaction includes gas production, temperature change, color change, light production, a new odor, a change in properties, or the formation of a precipitate. A precipitate is a solid that forms when substances in liquids react. However, evidence must be interpreted carefully. Boiling water makes bubbles, but the bubbles are water vapor, not a new substance. Mixing food coloring into water changes the color, but it does not by itself prove a chemical reaction. Strong scientific explanations use specific observations, such as a temperature rising from 22°C to 28°C or a white solid forming after two clear liquids are mixed.

questions.question: Why do bubbles in boiling water not prove a chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: They are bubbles of water vapor, and water vapor is still water, so no new substance has been shown to form.

questions.question: Give one example of a specific evidence statement from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: One example is that the temperature rose from 22°C to 28°C, or that a white solid formed after two clear liquids were mixed.

questions.question: Which combination would most strongly support that a chemical reaction occurred?
questions.modelAnswer: Several clues together, especially a new solid and temperature change, strongly support a chemical reaction.
options: A color change plus a new solid and temperature increase

data.sourceTitle: Atoms, Bonds, and Conservation of Mass
data.targetTitle: Atoms, Bonds, and Conservation of Mass
data.sourcePassage: During a chemical reaction, chemical bonds between atoms break and new bonds form. The atoms are rearranged, but the atoms themselves are conserved. The same kinds and numbers of atoms are present before and after the reaction. This explains the law of conservation of mass: matter is not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. In a closed system, the total mass of reactants and products should stay the same. In an open system, a gas product can escape, making the measured mass seem to decrease. The missing mass was not destroyed; it left the measured system as gas.

questions.question: What happens to atoms during a chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Atoms are rearranged into new combinations, but the atoms themselves are conserved.

questions.question: Which system best shows conservation of mass when gas forms?
questions.modelAnswer: A sealed bag is a closed system, so gas cannot escape.

questions.question: Why might the mass seem to decrease in an open cup reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: A gas product may escape into the air, so it is no longer part of what is measured.

questions.question: How are bonds involved in a chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Old bonds break and new bonds form as atoms rearrange into products.

questions.question: Which statement matches conservation of mass?
questions.modelAnswer: Conservation of mass means the same atoms are still present before and after the reaction.
options: The same atoms are present before and after the reaction

data.sourcePassage: Chemical reactions involve energy because chemical bonds store energy. An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings, so the surroundings may get warmer or light may be produced. Burning wood and many hand warmers are examples. An endothermic reaction absorbs energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings may get cooler. Some instant cold packs work this way. Reaction rate describes how fast reactants turn into products. Temperature, surface area, concentration, stirring, and catalysts can affect reaction rate. A crushed antacid tablet often reacts faster than a whole tablet because more surface area touches the water.

questions.question: What does reaction rate describe?
questions.modelAnswer: Reaction rate describes how fast reactants turn into products.

questions.modelAnswer: An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings.

questions.question: Why can crushing an antacid tablet make it react faster?
questions.modelAnswer: Crushing increases surface area, so more of the tablet can contact the water at once.

questions.question: How would warmer water usually affect particles in a reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Warmer water makes particles move faster and collide more often, which can speed up the reaction.

questions.question: Which set lists only reaction-rate factors from the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Those factors can affect how fast reactants turn into products.
options: Temperature, surface area, concentration, stirring, catalysts

data.sourceTitle: Using Data in a Fair Test
data.targetTitle: Using Data in a Fair Test
data.sourcePassage: A student tested how water temperature affects the time for an antacid tablet to stop fizzing. The same tablet type and water amount were used each time. At 10°C, fizzing stopped after 94 seconds. At 20°C, it stopped after 71 seconds. At 30°C, it stopped after 49 seconds. At 40°C, it stopped after 34 seconds. At 50°C, it stopped after 25 seconds. The pattern is clear: as temperature increases, reaction time decreases. A shorter reaction time means a faster reaction rate. To make the conclusion stronger, the student should repeat trials, keep controlled variables the same, and avoid unsafe temperatures.

questions.question: What was the independent variable in the antacid investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable was water temperature.

questions.question: What was the dependent variable?
questions.modelAnswer: The dependent variable was the time until fizzing stopped.

questions.question: At which listed temperature was the reaction fastest?
questions.modelAnswer: The reaction was fastest at 50°C because the fizzing stopped in the shortest time, 25 seconds.

questions.question: What pattern did the data show?
questions.modelAnswer: As water temperature increased, reaction time decreased, meaning the reaction rate increased.

questions.question: Why should the student repeat trials?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeating trials helps check reliability and reduces the effect of random errors or unusual results.

data.sourcePassage: Chemical reactions matter outside the classroom. Cooking an egg changes proteins so the clear liquid egg white becomes white and solid. Rusting happens when iron reacts with oxygen and water to form rust, a reddish-brown, flaky product that is weaker than iron. Engineers protect bridges, bicycles, cars, and ships by painting metal, coating it, using stainless steel, or keeping it dry. Combustion reactions release energy when fuels react with oxygen, but they can also affect air quality and climate. In the body, digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller molecules, and enzymes act as catalysts. In environmental cleanup, reactions can help remove harmful substances from water or make solids that can be filtered out.

questions.question: How can combustion be both useful and harmful?
questions.modelAnswer: Combustion provides useful energy, but it can also produce pollution and affect air quality or climate.

questions.question: What role do enzymes play in the body?
questions.modelAnswer: Enzymes act as catalysts that help chemical reactions happen at body temperature.
